lessons.title: Notation
lessons.subtitle: Read probability symbols like short sentences
lessons.introduction: Learn to read the symbols before using them. Each symbol names an outcome, a set, a probability, or a counting operation; keeping those roles separate prevents many later mistakes.
objectives: Recognize the symbols for outcomes, events, and set operations.
Read probability, conditional probability, sums, and products aloud.
Distinguish counting notation from probability notation.

concepts.title: Outcomes, sample spaces, and events
concepts.explanation: Ω is the set of all possible outcomes. A lowercase ω names one outcome; an uppercase A names an event, which is a set of outcomes. The symbol ∈ means “is an element of,” while ⊆ means “is a subset of.” Thus ω ∈ A compares an outcome with a set, and A ⊆ Ω compares two sets. ∅ is the empty set: it contains no outcomes.
concepts.formula: ω ∈ A ⊆ Ω; ∅ = empty set; A = B means the same elements

example.title: Tomorrow’s weather
example.situation: Suppose tomorrow can be sunny, cloudy, or rainy.
walkthrough: Write Ω = {sunny, cloudy, rainy}.
Let A = {cloudy, rainy}, the event “the sky is not clear.”
The statement rainy ∈ A is true because rainy appears in that set.
example.result: Ω is the complete list; A is the smaller collection that answers the question we care about.

concepts.remember: Ω contains possibilities. An event selects some of them.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not confuse ∅ with {0}. The empty set has no outcomes; {0} contains one outcome named 0.

concepts.title: Or, and, and not
concepts.explanation: These symbols combine sets. A ∪ B includes outcomes in A, in B, or in both. A ∩ B includes only outcomes in both. Aᶜ includes the outcomes in Ω that are outside A. The superscript c means complement, not a power. Always specify Ω before taking a complement.
concepts.formula: A ∪ B: A or B (including both)   ·   A ∩ B: A and B   ·   Aᶜ: not A

example.title: Choosing a café
example.situation: You list cafés that are nearby and cafés that are open late.
walkthrough: A = cafés nearby.
B = cafés open late.
A ∩ B contains cafés that satisfy both needs. A ∪ B also includes cafés that satisfy only one.
example.result: Use intersection when every requirement must be satisfied; use union when either requirement is enough.

concepts.remember: The word “or” is inclusive unless the situation explicitly says “exactly one.”
concepts.commonMistake: A ∪ B is not just the part unique to each event; it also includes the overlap.

concepts.title: Probability and conditioning
concepts.explanation: P turns an event into a number between 0 and 1. P(A ∩ B) asks for both events to occur. P(A | B) asks for A after learning that B occurred: the vertical bar means “given,” not division. The condition B must have positive probability for this ratio definition.
concepts.formula: P(A | B) is read “the probability of A given B.”

example.title: A train during rush hour
example.situation: Let A be “the train is crowded” and B be “you travel at 8:00 a.m.”
walkthrough: P(A) uses trips at every time of day.
P(A | B) keeps only trips made at 8:00 a.m.
The two probabilities can differ because the second question uses a narrower group of trips.
example.result: The vertical bar means that the information after it is already known.

concepts.remember: Read the condition first: given B, ask about A.
concepts.commonMistake: P(A | B) and P(B | A) ask different questions and usually have different values.

concepts.title: Lists, sums, and products
concepts.explanation: An index tells you which term you are using: p₁ is the first probability, p₂ the second. Σ means add; ∏ means multiply. Read the lower and upper limits to find the first and last indices. Similarly, ⋃ combines a list of sets by union and ⋂ combines them by intersection.
concepts.formula: Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ pᵢ = p₁ + ··· + pₙ   ·   ∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿ pᵢ = p₁ × ··· × pₙ

example.title: Three delivery stages
example.situation: A parcel must pass sorting, transport, and final delivery.
walkthrough: Label the success probabilities p₁, p₂, and p₃.
Σᵢ₌₁³ pᵢ adds the three numbers; it does not describe all stages succeeding.
When the stages are independent, ∏ᵢ₌₁³ pᵢ gives the probability that all three succeed.
example.result: The shape of the symbol tells you whether to add or multiply.

concepts.remember: Σ means add; ∏ means multiply.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not use a product merely because several probabilities are present. Multiplication needs the right event structure and, often, independence.

concepts.title: Counting symbols
concepts.explanation: |A| is the number of elements in a finite set A. The factorial n! multiplies the integers from 1 through n, with 0! defined as 1. C(n,k), also written as n above k in parentheses, counts selections of k distinct objects from n when their order does not matter. These symbols count possibilities; they become probabilities only after a model is specified.

example.title: Choosing two lunch representatives
example.situation: Five coworkers will choose two people to collect lunch.
walkthrough: There are 5 choices for the first name and 4 for the second.
Each pair was counted twice because Alex–Sam and Sam–Alex are the same team.
example.result: Use combinations for an unordered team and factorial-based arrangements when positions matter.

concepts.remember: Ask whether changing the order creates a new result before choosing a counting formula.
concepts.commonMistake: Using 5×4=20 for an unordered pair counts every pair twice.

quickChecks.explanation: Intersection contains exactly the outcomes shared by both events.
Capital pi means multiply the indicated terms.

lessons.title: Sets and events
lessons.subtitle: Describe uncertain situations precisely
lessons.introduction: Begin with sets: what they contain, how they combine, and when a collection forms a partition. Then interpret events using those same set operations. No probability calculations are needed yet.
objectives: Build a sample space and events from a situation.
Combine events with union, intersection, and complement.
Recognize disjoint events and partitions.
Use De Morgan’s laws to negate combined events.

concepts.title: Sample spaces and events
concepts.explanation: A set is defined by its elements, not by their order or by how many times a name is written. In probability, Ω is the full set of possible outcomes and an event A is a subset of Ω. An event occurs when the actual outcome belongs to it. The empty event ∅ never occurs; Ω always occurs. A ⊆ B means every outcome in A is also in B, possibly with A = B.

example.title: A takeaway order
example.situation: A customer chooses one drink: tea, coffee, or water.
walkthrough: Set Ω = {tea, coffee, water}.
Let A be “the drink contains caffeine,” so A = {tea, coffee}.
When the customer chooses water, event A does not occur.
example.result: The outcome is one selected drink; the event groups the outcomes with the property we care about.

concepts.remember: An event can contain one outcome, several outcomes, all outcomes, or none.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not list probabilities inside Ω. The sample space lists outcomes; the probability law assigns their chances.
concepts.definition: A set is a collection of objects, which are the elements of the set.

concepts.title: Combining events
concepts.explanation: The word “or” is inclusive in a union: doing both still qualifies. An intersection requires both conditions. A complement contains everything in the chosen sample space that fails the condition. To translate a sentence into sets, decide which outcomes satisfy it before calculating any probabilities.

example.title: Weekend plans
example.situation: Let A be “visit a park” and B be “meet a friend.”
walkthrough: A ∪ B occurs if you do either activity or both.
A ∩ B occurs only if you do both.
Aᶜ occurs if you do not visit a park, regardless of whether you meet a friend.
example.result: Translate the sentence first, then apply the matching set operation.

concepts.remember: “At least one” almost always signals a union.
concepts.commonMistake: Complement applies to the whole event immediately before the superscript, so parentheses matter.
concepts.definition: The union of two sets S and T is the set of all elements that belong to S or T (or both), and is denoted by S ∪ T.

concepts.title: Disjoint events
concepts.explanation: Disjoint sets have no shared element. For events, that means no single experimental outcome makes both events occur. This describes the structure of the events; it does not say that they have equal probabilities or that they are independent. More than two sets are disjoint when every pair has an empty intersection.

example.title: One bus arrival time
example.situation: A bus is classified as early, on time, or late.
walkthrough: Let A be “early” and B be “late.”
A single arrival cannot be both early and late.
Therefore A ∩ B = ∅.
example.result: Disjointness is about impossibility of simultaneous occurrence.

concepts.remember: Disjoint events have no shared outcomes.
concepts.commonMistake: Disjoint does not mean equally likely, and it does not usually mean independent.
concepts.definition: Two sets are said to be disjoint if their intersection is empty.

concepts.title: Partitions
concepts.explanation: A partition divides a set into separate groups that cover it completely. Check two requirements: no outcome belongs to two groups, and no outcome is left out. Braces name a collection of groups; a union combines their elements into one set. When the groups partition Ω, their union must be exactly Ω. The groups need not have equal sizes or equal probabilities.
concepts.formula: Cover all of Ω · No overlap between any two groups

example.title: Partition versus non-partition
example.situation: A shop classifies deliveries by arrival time. Let Ω contain all deliveries, E the early ones, T the on-time ones, and L the late ones. These categories use agreed time boundaries, so each delivery has exactly one time label. Let F contain fragile deliveries. Here are three deliveries to compare.
walkthrough: Partition: {E, T, L}, where E = early, T = on time, and L = late.
Every delivery is early, on time, or late, and no delivery can be in two of these groups. Therefore E ∪ T ∪ L = Ω: joining the three groups gives all deliveries.
Non-partition: {E, T, L, F}, where F is the set of fragile deliveries.
A fragile delivery is also early, on time, or late. It belongs to F and to one of the other three groups, so it appears twice. Therefore {E, T, L, F} is not a partition.
There is another way to fail: {E, T} has no overlap, but leaves all late deliveries out. Coverage matters as well as separation.
example.result: {E, T, L} is a partition because every delivery appears exactly once. {E, T, L, F} is not a partition because every fragile delivery appears in two groups.

concepts.remember: For every outcome, count how many groups contain it. A partition requires the answer to be exactly one every time.
concepts.commonMistake: Groups can have different names and still overlap. Arrival status and package type describe different properties, so a fragile delivery can also be early, on time, or late.
concepts.definition: A collection of sets is said to be a partition of a set S if the sets in the collection are disjoint and their union is S.

concepts.title: De Morgan’s laws
concepts.explanation: To be outside a union, an outcome must be outside both sets. To be outside an intersection, it only needs to be outside at least one set. This is why taking a complement switches ∪ and ∩. The two rules describe different events: “neither” is more restrictive than “not both.”
concepts.formula: (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ · (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ

example.title: Rain and strong wind
example.situation: Let A mean “it rains” and B mean “there is strong wind.”
walkthrough: A ∪ B means there is rain, strong wind, or both.
To make A ∪ B false, rain must be absent and strong wind must also be absent.
Therefore (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ: “no rain and no strong wind.”
A ∩ B means both hazards occur. Its complement allows any case where at least one hazard is absent: (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ.
example.result: “Not either” means neither one. “Not both” means at least one is absent.

concepts.remember: When the complement moves inside parentheses, negate each event and flip ∪ to ∩ or ∩ to ∪.
concepts.commonMistake: “Not rain or wind” is ambiguous in ordinary speech. Use parentheses first, then translate: not (rain or wind) means no rain and no wind.

quickChecks.prompt: Every order has exactly one size: small, medium, or large. Why do these three groups form a partition?
options: Every order is in exactly one group
All three groups are equally likely
An order can be in several groups
quickChecks.correctAnswer: Every order is in exactly one group
quickChecks.explanation: The groups cover all orders and do not overlap, which are the two requirements for a partition.

quickChecks.prompt: What is the complement of “rain or strong wind”?
options: No rain or no strong wind
No rain and no strong wind
quickChecks.correctAnswer: No rain and no strong wind
quickChecks.explanation: By De Morgan’s law, the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements.

lessons.title: Building a probability model
lessons.subtitle: Choose outcomes and assign valid probabilities
lessons.introduction: Build a model in two stages: choose outcomes that distinguish what matters, then assign a consistent probability law. Use trees when the experiment unfolds in stages, and keep the model’s assumptions visible.
objectives: Choose a useful sample space for a question.
Apply nonnegativity, normalization, and additivity.
Handle finite and countably infinite outcome sets.
Represent sequential outcomes with a tree and distinguish model assumptions from facts.

concepts.title: The two parts of a model
concepts.explanation: First specify an experiment: the process whose result is uncertain. Then list its mutually exclusive possible outcomes in Ω. Finally assign a probability law to events. An outcome describes what happens; a probability describes how likely a collection of outcomes is under the model. Different probability laws can be placed on the same sample space.
concepts.formula: Model = sample space Ω + probability law P

example.title: A delivery window
example.situation: A parcel can arrive in the morning, afternoon, or evening.
walkthrough: Choose Ω = {morning, afternoon, evening}.
Assign probabilities such as 0.3, 0.5, and 0.2.
Check that every number is nonnegative and that 0.3+0.5+0.2=1.
example.result: The outcomes describe the possibilities; the probabilities describe your uncertainty about them.

concepts.remember: Always state both what can happen and how likely it is.
concepts.commonMistake: A list of outcomes alone is not yet a complete probability model.
concepts.definition: A probabilistic model is a mathematical description of an uncertain situation.

concepts.title: Choose enough detail
concepts.explanation: An outcome must settle every question you intend to ask. Outcomes must also be distinct and mutually exclusive: one performance of the experiment produces exactly one outcome. A coarse description can be useful, but it may erase distinctions that matter. Choose the level of detail before assigning probabilities.

example.title: What did the customer order?
example.situation: A café records whether one customer buys a drink and whether they buy a cake. You want to answer both “How many items?” and “Was a drink purchased?”
walkthrough: Use Ω = {(no drink, no cake), (drink, no cake), (no drink, cake), (drink, cake)}. Exactly one pair describes the visit.
Recording only the item count gives {0, 1, 2}. But one item could mean a drink or a cake.
The count-only model answers the first question. The pair model answers both questions.
example.result: Choose the pair model when the identity of the item matters.

concepts.remember: Keep every distinction that can change the event of interest.
concepts.commonMistake: The smallest-looking sample space is not always the most useful one.
concepts.definition: In addition, the sample space should have enough detail to distinguish between all outcomes of interest to the modeler, while avoiding irrelevant details.

concepts.title: The probability axioms
concepts.explanation: The three rules work together. Nonnegativity forbids negative probability. Normalization assigns probability 1 to Ω. Additivity says probabilities of disjoint events can be added, because no outcome is counted twice. For countably many disjoint events, use the corresponding infinite sum. Addition without checking disjointness is not justified by this axiom.

example.title: Payment outcomes
example.situation: A checkout is successful, declined, or abandoned with probabilities 0.72, 0.18, and 0.10.
walkthrough: All three probabilities are nonnegative.
The outcomes are disjoint.
Their probabilities total 1, so the assignment is valid.
example.result: The probability of “not successful” is 0.18+0.10=0.28.

concepts.remember: Disjoint probabilities add because the same outcome is never counted twice.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding probabilities of overlapping events double-counts their shared outcomes.
concepts.definition: In order to visualize a probability law, consider a unit of mass which is to be “spread” over the sample space. Then, P(A) is simply the total mass that was assigned collectively to the elements of A.

concepts.title: Finite and countably infinite models
concepts.explanation: A finite model has a last item on its list of possible outcomes. A countably infinite model has an endless list, such as 1, 2, 3, … . In either case, assign a probability to each individual outcome and add the masses of outcomes in an event. For an infinite list, the infinite sum must equal 1. This is different from assigning equal positive probability to infinitely many outcomes, which cannot total 1.
concepts.formula: For disjoint A₁,A₂,…: P(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ)=Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)

example.title: Attempts until an upload succeeds
example.situation: Assume each upload independently succeeds with probability 1/2. Record the attempt number of the first success.
walkthrough: Success immediately has probability 1/2. One failure then success has probability (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4.
Two failures then success has probability 1/8. In general the first success on attempt k has probability (1/2)^k.
The masses sum to 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1. Eventual success has probability 1 under this model.
example.result: The count has infinitely many possible values, but each has a well-defined probability.

concepts.remember: Countably infinite outcomes can be indexed as a sequence.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not assume an infinite sample space gives each individual outcome probability zero; that is a feature of many continuous models, not every infinite model.
concepts.definition: If the sample space consists of a finite number of possible outcomes, then the probability law is specified by the probabilities of the events that consist of a single element.

concepts.title: Sequential experiments and trees
concepts.explanation: A multistage experiment can be represented as a tree. A node records the history so far; each outgoing branch is a possible next result. A complete root-to-leaf path is one outcome of the whole experiment. Branches at the same node must cover all possibilities without overlap. The tree keeps order and earlier results visible.
concepts.formula: Outcome = one complete path through the tree

example.title: Two contacts from a support team
example.situation: A support worker calls two customers in order. Each answers (A) or does not answer (N).
walkthrough: The first call branches into A and N. From each branch, the second call again branches into A and N.
The leaves are AA, AN, NA, and NN. AN and NA are distinct because different customers answered.
The event “exactly one answer” contains two leaves: AN and NA.
example.result: A tree reveals all four outcomes and prevents a count such as “one answer” from hiding different paths.

concepts.remember: A leaf describes the full experiment, not just its final stage.
concepts.commonMistake: The number of branches alone does not establish that their probabilities are equal.

concepts.title: A model and the situation it describes
concepts.explanation: Probability rules tell us whether a model is mathematically consistent. They do not establish that its assumptions accurately describe reality. The sample space and probability law are choices informed by the situation, observations, or symmetry. A valid calculation is a conclusion conditional on those choices.

example.title: A delivery forecast
example.situation: A shop models delivery as morning, afternoon, or evening, with probabilities 0.3, 0.5, and 0.2.
walkthrough: The numbers are nonnegative and sum to 1, so they form a valid probability assignment.
The model predicts a 0.8 chance of delivery by the end of the afternoon.
If a new courier or a holiday changes arrival patterns, the same arithmetic remains valid but the assigned probabilities may need updating.
example.result: Check the assumptions as well as the calculation.

concepts.remember: A probability is part of a specified model.
concepts.commonMistake: Probabilities summing to 1 does not prove that the model matches the situation.

quickChecks.prompt: Which assignment is a valid probability law for three disjoint outcomes?
quickChecks.explanation: The values are nonnegative and sum to 1.

quickChecks.prompt: Why is recording only the number of heads insufficient when asking whether the first toss was heads?
options: The count loses the order of tosses
The first toss has probability zero
quickChecks.correctAnswer: The count loses the order of tosses
quickChecks.explanation: Different sequences can have the same total number of heads.

lessons.title: Calculating event probabilities
lessons.subtitle: Count outcomes, avoid double-counting, and use geometry
lessons.introduction: Use the probability axioms to calculate events. Start with equally likely finite outcomes, then use complements, overlapping sets, geometric probability, and bounds when exact calculation is harder.
objectives: Use favorable outcomes over total outcomes when outcomes are equally likely.
Apply complements and inclusion–exclusion.
Interpret uniform continuous probability as length or area.
Bound a union probability when its overlap is unknown.

concepts.title: Equally likely outcomes
concepts.explanation: Counting gives probability only when the elementary outcomes in a finite sample space are equally likely. If there are n of them, each has mass 1/n. An event containing k outcomes then has probability k/n. Grouping elementary outcomes into larger categories can destroy equal likelihood: “zero, one, or two successes” need not be three equally likely events.

example.title: Picking a weekday
example.situation: One of the five workdays is selected uniformly for a meeting.
walkthrough: There are |Ω|=5 possible days.
The event “Monday or Friday” has |A|=2 outcomes.
example.result: Count only after confirming that every listed outcome is equally likely.

concepts.remember: The counting shortcut depends on equal likelihood.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not use favorable divided by total when outcomes have different probabilities.

concepts.title: Use the complement for “at least one”
concepts.explanation: A and Aᶜ are disjoint and together cover Ω. Additivity therefore gives P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = 1. Use this when the complement has fewer cases to count. In particular, the opposite of “at least one” is “none,” not “all.” No independence assumption is needed for the complement rule itself.

example.title: At least one busy checkout
example.situation: A store observes 100 equally weighted snapshots of two checkouts. In 35 snapshots both are free. You choose one snapshot uniformly.
walkthrough: Let A mean at least one checkout is busy.
Aᶜ means neither is busy: both are free. Its probability is 35/100 = 0.35.
example.result: The probability is 65%, without needing to assume independent checkout activity.

concepts.remember: For “at least one,” first check whether “none” is easier.
concepts.commonMistake: Subtract the probability of the exact complement, not merely one unwanted case.

concepts.title: Correct for overlap
concepts.explanation: The union contains A-only outcomes, B-only outcomes, and the overlap. Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice; subtract P(A ∩ B) once to retain it exactly once. For disjoint events that correction is zero, recovering ordinary addition. Sketching or listing the three regions often makes the formula clear.

example.title: Customers using two features
example.situation: 60% use search, 50% use filters, and 20% use both.
walkthrough: Adding 0.60+0.50 gives 1.10 because shared users appear twice.
Subtract the overlap 0.20 once.
P(search or filters)=0.60+0.50−0.20=0.90.
example.result: Inclusion–exclusion removes double-counting.

concepts.remember: If the overlap is unknown, P(A∪B)≤P(A)+P(B) is still a useful upper bound.
concepts.commonMistake: Probabilities above 1 are a strong sign that overlap was not handled correctly.

concepts.title: Uniform length and area
concepts.explanation: For a uniform point on a continuous interval, probability is a length fraction; for a uniform point in a region, it is an area fraction. There is no finite list of equally likely points to count. A single point has zero length or area, so it has probability zero even though the experiment must produce some point. Probability zero does not always mean an empty event.
concepts.formula: Probability = favorable length or area ÷ total length or area

example.title: A random arrival time
example.situation: A visitor arrives uniformly between 2:00 and 3:00 p.m.
walkthrough: The full interval is 60 minutes long.
The event 2:15–2:30 is 15 minutes long.
Its probability is 15/60=1/4.
example.result: A single exact instant has zero length, so its probability is zero in this model.

concepts.remember: Uniform probability follows relative size: count, length, area, or volume.
concepts.commonMistake: Probability zero does not mean logically impossible in a continuous model; an exact point can occur even though it has zero length.

concepts.title: Probability bounds
concepts.explanation: If A is contained in B, every outcome counted by A is also counted by B, so P(A) cannot exceed P(B). For a union, adding all the event probabilities can overcount shared outcomes but cannot miss any outcome in the union. This gives an upper bound even when overlaps are unknown.
concepts.formula: A ⊆ B ⇒ P(A) ≤ P(B); P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A) + P(B)

example.title: Two possible delivery problems
example.situation: A parcel has a 10% chance of delay and a 4% chance of damage. Their overlap is unknown.
walkthrough: “Delayed” is contained in “delayed or damaged,” so the union probability is at least 10%.
The union bound gives at most 10% + 4% = 14%.
If every damaged parcel is delayed, the union is 10%. If none is both, it is 14%.
example.result: The probability of at least one problem lies between 10% and 14%.

concepts.remember: A bound can be useful when an exact overlap is unavailable.
concepts.commonMistake: Using 14% as the exact answer assumes that delay and damage are disjoint.

concepts.title: Uniform probability on a region
concepts.explanation: A pair of continuous measurements can be represented by a point in a plane. Under a uniform model on a region, a subregion’s probability is its area divided by the whole area. Translate the event into a geometric region before calculating. This model assumes equal probability per unit area, not merely that each coordinate has a particular range.

example.title: Two friends meeting for coffee
example.situation: Two friends independently arrive uniformly during a 60-minute window. Each will wait 15 minutes for the other. Let x and y be their arrival times in minutes after the window starts.
walkthrough: The sample space is a 60-by-60 square of area 3,600. They meet when |x − y| ≤ 15.
Failure occupies two corner triangles: x exceeds y by more than 15, or y exceeds x by more than 15. Each triangle has perpendicular sides of length 45.
The failure area is 2 × (45 × 45/2) = 2,025. The meeting probability is 1 − 2,025/3,600 = 7/16 = 43.75%.
example.result: Draw the failure region first: two simple triangles are easier to measure than the diagonal meeting strip.

concepts.remember: Uniform probability in two dimensions uses area.
concepts.commonMistake: A 15-minute waiting limit does not give 15/60 directly; the event depends on two arrival times.

quickChecks.prompt: P(A)=0.7, P(B)=0.4, and P(A∩B)=0.2. What is P(A∪B)?
A time is chosen uniformly from a 40-minute window. What is the probability it falls in a specified 10-minute subwindow?
quickChecks.explanation: The favorable length is 10 out of 40 minutes.

lessons.title: Conditional probability
lessons.subtitle: Update the sample space when new information arrives
lessons.introduction: Information changes the universe in which a probability is calculated. Learn to restrict and renormalize, distinguish the two directions of a conditional, and multiply probabilities along a sequence.
objectives: Interpret conditioning as restricting the sample space.
Calculate conditional probabilities and path probabilities.
Model sequential choices with and without replacement.

concepts.title: Conditioning narrows the world
concepts.explanation: Learning B rules out outcomes outside B. Keep the original relative probabilities inside B, then rescale their total from P(B) to 1. The part of B that also satisfies A is A ∩ B, giving P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). This creates a new probability law on the restricted universe B. The ratio is defined only when P(B) > 0.

example.title: A delivery is known to be late
example.situation: Choose one of 100 deliveries uniformly. There are 20 late deliveries, and 8 of those came from warehouse A. Let L mean late and A mean from warehouse A.
walkthrough: Before the information, the late-and-A group has probability 8/100. The late group has probability 20/100.
Given L, the 80 on-time deliveries leave the comparison group. The remaining 20 deliveries are the new universe.
P(A | L) = (8/100)/(20/100) = 8/20 = 0.40. The other 12 late deliveries carry probability 0.60.
example.result: Within the late group, 40% came from warehouse A; the conditional probabilities total 1.

concepts.remember: After “given,” rebuild the denominator from the remaining possibilities.
concepts.commonMistake: Keeping the original denominator would ignore the information you were given.
concepts.definition: Conditional probability provides us with a way to reason about the outcome of an experiment, based on partial information.

concepts.title: The order of the condition matters
concepts.explanation: The event after the bar determines the comparison group. P(A | B) divides the overlap by P(B); P(B | A) divides the same overlap by P(A). Their numerators agree but their denominators generally do not. Neither conditional can be read from the other without information about the sizes or probabilities of those groups.

example.title: The same deliveries, two questions
example.situation: Of 100 deliveries, 40 came from warehouse A, 20 were late, and 8 were both from A and late.
walkthrough: Among late deliveries, the warehouse-A share is P(A | L) = 8/20 = 40%.
Among warehouse-A deliveries, the late share is P(L | A) = 8/40 = 20%.
Both questions use the same 8 deliveries, but compare them with different groups.
example.result: 40% and 20% answer different questions; reversing the bar changes the denominator.

concepts.remember: Say “among B cases, the fraction that are A” when interpreting P(A | B).
concepts.commonMistake: A strong effect of B on A does not automatically make A strong evidence for B.

concepts.title: Multiply along a sequence
concepts.explanation: Rearranging the definition of conditional probability gives the multiplication rule. For a longer path, each next probability is conditional on the full history along that path. Multiply along a path to obtain a joint probability; add the probabilities of disjoint paths to obtain an event probability. Independence is not required when the correct conditional probabilities are used.

example.title: A two-stage application
example.situation: 40% of applications pass screening; among those, 30% pass the interview.
walkthrough: P(screening)=0.40.
P(interview | screening)=0.30.
example.result: Conditional branches multiply along a path.

concepts.remember: Use the probability written on each branch after the history leading to it.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding branch probabilities along a single path is incorrect; addition combines alternative paths.
concepts.definition: We obtain the probability of a leaf by multiplying the probabilities recorded along the corresponding path of the tree.

concepts.title: Without replacement changes the next probability
concepts.explanation: Drawing without replacement changes which items remain. Condition on the earlier result, update the contents, then calculate the next branch probability using the new total. The multiplication rule still applies; it is the second factor that changes. Drawing with replacement would be a different experiment.

example.title: Two red markers
example.situation: A box contains 3 red and 2 blue markers. Two are chosen without replacement.
walkthrough: P(first red)=3/5.
After a red is removed, 2 red markers remain among 4 total, so P(second red | first red)=2/4.
example.result: The second fraction changes because the first draw changes the box.

concepts.remember: Update both the favorable count and the total count after every draw without replacement.
concepts.commonMistake: Using 3/5 for both draws silently treats the draws as if the marker were replaced.

quickChecks.prompt: A fair die is known to show a number greater than 3. What is P(6 | greater than 3)?
quickChecks.explanation: The remaining equally likely outcomes are {4,5,6}.

quickChecks.prompt: 50% pass stage one and 20% of those pass stage two. What fraction pass both?

lessons.title: Total probability and Bayes’ rule
lessons.subtitle: Combine possible causes, then reason backward from evidence
lessons.introduction: Combine conditional models by splitting Ω into scenarios. Total probability adds their contributions; Bayes’ rule uses the resulting total to update the probabilities of the scenarios after evidence.
objectives: Break a problem into disjoint cases and combine them.
Use Bayes’ rule to infer a cause from an observation.
Account for base rates when interpreting evidence.

concepts.title: Divide the world into cases
concepts.explanation: Start with disjoint scenarios that cover Ω. Within each scenario Aᵢ, calculate the chance of B. Multiply by P(Aᵢ) to return that conditional probability to its share of the whole sample space. Finally add the disjoint pieces Aᵢ ∩ B. This is a weighted average, with scenario probabilities as the weights; omit zero-probability cases from conditional calculations.

example.title: Commuting by train or bicycle
example.situation: You take the train 70% of days and cycle 30%. You arrive late on 10% of train days and 5% of cycling days.
walkthrough: Late by bicycle: 0.30×0.05=0.015.
example.result: The weighted average uses how often each commuting method occurs.

concepts.remember: Multiply within each case, then add across alternative cases.
concepts.commonMistake: A simple average of 10% and 5% would be wrong because the two commuting methods are not equally common.
concepts.definition: Then, the probability that B occurs is a weighted average of its conditional probability under each scenario, where each scenario is weighted according to its (unconditional) probability.

concepts.title: Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional
concepts.explanation: The prior P(Aᵢ) describes a scenario before the evidence. The likelihood P(B | Aᵢ) describes how often that scenario produces the evidence. Multiply them to obtain P(Aᵢ ∩ B), then divide by the total evidence probability P(B). The result P(Aᵢ | B) is the posterior: the share of the evidence attributable to that scenario. Require P(B) > 0.

example.title: A late parcel
example.situation: Warehouse A handles 80% of parcels and is late 2% of the time. Warehouse B handles 20% and is late 8% of the time.
walkthrough: Among all late parcels, B’s share is 0.016/(0.016+0.016)=1/2.
example.result: B handles fewer parcels, but its higher late rate makes the two causes equally likely after observing a delay.

concepts.remember: Posterior probability is proportional to prior probability × likelihood.
concepts.commonMistake: Choosing the cause with the largest error rate ignores how common that cause is.
concepts.definition: Bayes’ rule is often used for inference. There are a number of “causes” that may result in a certain “effect.”

concepts.title: Base rates matter
concepts.explanation: A strong signal does not by itself tell us the probability of its cause. We must count signals from every possible cause, including common alternatives. Converting percentages into a hypothetical population makes the denominator visible. The resulting counts are model-based expected counts, not additional observations.

example.title: A device alarm
example.situation: Only 1% of devices are faulty. An alarm sounds for 90% of faulty devices and 10% of working devices.
walkthrough: Out of 10,000 devices, expect 100 faulty and 9,900 working.
About 90 faulty devices and 990 working devices trigger alarms.
Among 1,080 alarms, only 90 indicate a fault: 90/1,080≈8.3%.
example.result: The alarm is informative, but false alarms from the much larger working group dominate.

concepts.remember: Translate percentages into expected counts when Bayes calculations feel unintuitive.
concepts.commonMistake: Accuracy within the rare group is not the same as the probability of the rare cause after a positive signal.

concepts.title: Build a cause-and-evidence tree
concepts.explanation: Place the scenarios first and the evidence second in a tree. Each complete path has a joint probability. Once the evidence is known, retain only paths compatible with it and divide each retained path probability by their total. Total probability builds the denominator; Bayes’ rule selects a scenario’s share of it.

example.title: Choosing an opponent
example.situation: You face a beginner 75% of the time and an expert 25%. You win 80% against beginners and 20% against experts.
walkthrough: Beginner-and-win path: 0.75×0.80=0.60.
Expert-and-win path: 0.25×0.20=0.05.
Given that you won, P(beginner)=0.60/(0.60+0.05)=12/13.
example.result: Only paths compatible with the observed win belong in the final denominator.

concepts.remember: Label every branch with a conditional probability appropriate to the path leading to it.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not place P(cause | evidence) on the forward tree before it has been calculated.

quickChecks.prompt: A shop uses supplier A for 60% of items with a 2% defect rate and B for 40% with a 5% defect rate. What fraction are defective?
What quantity does Bayes’ rule produce after observing evidence B?
quickChecks.explanation: Bayes’ rule updates the probability of a cause or hypothesis A after observing B.

lessons.title: Independence
lessons.subtitle: Recognize when one event gives no information about another
lessons.introduction: Define independence using probabilities, distinguish it from disjointness, and check what happens after conditioning or when more than two events are involved.
objectives: Test independence using products or conditional probabilities.
Distinguish independence from disjointness.
Separate pairwise, mutual, and conditional independence.

concepts.title: Testing independence
concepts.explanation: Independence is a property of two events under a probability law. If learning B does not change A’s probability, then P(A | B) = P(A), when P(B) > 0. Multiplying by P(B) gives the symmetric product test below. The product test also handles zero-probability events, for which a conditional ratio may be undefined. The model must justify independence; different event names do not.

example.title: Two separate coin tosses
example.situation: A is “the first toss is heads” and B is “the second toss is heads.”
walkthrough: Because 1/4=(1/2)(1/2), the events are independent.
example.result: Knowing the first toss does not change the chance of heads on the second toss.

concepts.remember: Independence can be checked with either P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) or P(A | B)=P(A) when the condition is defined.
concepts.commonMistake: Similar-looking probabilities are not enough; test the defining equality.
concepts.definition: The symmetry of this relation also implies that independence is a symmetric property; that is, if A is independent of B, then B is independent of A, and we can unambiguously say that A and B are independent events.

concepts.title: Disjoint is different from independent
concepts.explanation: If two positive-probability events are disjoint, learning that one occurred makes the other impossible. That changes its probability, so the events cannot be independent. Independence means information about one leaves the chance of the other unchanged; disjointness means their intersection is empty. These are different mathematical conditions.
concepts.formula: Disjoint: A ∩ B = ∅ · Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)

example.title: One restaurant order
example.situation: A is “the main dish is pasta” and B is “the main dish is curry.”
walkthrough: A and B are disjoint because one main dish cannot be both.
If both dishes have positive probability, P(A)P(B)>0.
But P(A∩B)=0, so the events are not independent.
example.result: Learning that pasta was ordered makes curry impossible, so the events strongly affect each other.

concepts.remember: Positive-probability disjoint events are dependent.
concepts.commonMistake: Everyday speech sometimes uses “independent” to mean separate; probability uses a strict mathematical definition.
concepts.definition: A common first thought is that two events are independent if they are disjoint, but in fact the opposite is true: two disjoint events A and B with P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0 are never independent, since their intersection A ∩ B is empty and has probability 0.

concepts.title: Conditional independence
concepts.explanation: Conditional independence asks the same question inside a restricted universe C. Compare P(A ∩ B | C) with P(A | C)P(B | C), assuming P(C) > 0. A shared background factor can make two events dependent overall even when they are independent within each background group. Conversely, selecting a group based on both events can introduce dependence.

example.title: A shared delivery-day condition
example.situation: Half of delivery days are dry and half are stormy. Two parcels are conditionally independent given the day’s weather. On dry days each is late with probability 0.1; on stormy days each is late with probability 0.5.
walkthrough: Each parcel is late with probability 0.5 × 0.1 + 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.3.
Both are late with probability 0.5 × 0.1² + 0.5 × 0.5² = 0.13. This differs from 0.3² = 0.09, so the events are dependent overall.
Within dry days, P(both late | dry) = 0.01 = 0.1 × 0.1. Within stormy days it is 0.25 = 0.5 × 0.5.
example.result: Fixing the shared weather makes the events independent in this model, but mixing the two groups makes them dependent.

concepts.remember: Always state the conditioning event when claiming conditional independence.
concepts.commonMistake: Unconditional independence and conditional independence do not imply each other in general.

concepts.title: Pairwise versus mutual independence
concepts.explanation: Pairwise independence checks every two-event intersection. Mutual independence checks every subcollection, including triples and larger groups. For three events, the three pairwise equations are not enough: the triple intersection must also equal the product of all three probabilities. Information from two events together may reveal something that neither reveals alone.

example.title: Two coin tosses and whether they match
example.situation: A is “first toss is heads,” B is “second toss is heads,” and C is “the tosses match.”
walkthrough: The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, and TT. Each event A, B, C contains two outcomes, so each probability is 1/2.
Each pairwise intersection contains only HH. Every pair therefore has overlap 1/4 = (1/2)(1/2).
The triple intersection is also {HH}, with probability 1/4. But the three-probability product is (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Knowing A and B together forces C, even though knowing either alone does not change its probability.
example.result: The three events are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.

concepts.remember: For several events, pairwise checks are necessary but may not be sufficient.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not stop after checking only pairs when a problem asks whether the entire collection is independent.
concepts.definition: Independence means that the occurrence or non-occurrence of any number of the events from that collection carries no information on the remaining events or their complements.

quickChecks.prompt: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, and P(A∩B)=0.2. Are A and B independent?
quickChecks.explanation: The product 0.4×0.5 equals the observed overlap 0.2.

quickChecks.prompt: Two disjoint events both have positive probability. What must be true?
quickChecks.explanation: Occurrence of either event makes the other impossible.

lessons.title: Independent trials and reliability
lessons.subtitle: Model repeated attempts and systems made from components
lessons.introduction: Apply independence to repeated trials and systems of components. Separate the probability of one pattern from the probability of a success count, and compare series with parallel arrangements.
objectives: Recognize independent Bernoulli trials.
Calculate exact success counts with binomial probabilities.
Analyze series and parallel reliability systems.

concepts.title: Independent Bernoulli trials
concepts.explanation: A Bernoulli trial records success or failure. In an independent sequence with common success probability p, every fixed pattern has probability equal to the product of its factors. A pattern containing k successes and n − k failures has probability pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, regardless of their positions. Calling an outcome “success” is just a label; it can represent a fault or a delay.
concepts.formula: P(a specific sequence with k successes in n trials)=pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ

example.title: Three notification deliveries
example.situation: Each notification arrives with probability 0.8, independently.
walkthrough: The specific pattern success, success, failure has two successes and one failure.
Multiply along the pattern: 0.8×0.8×0.2.
Its probability is 0.128.
example.result: A specific pattern uses multiplication; an unspecified count also needs the number of matching patterns.

concepts.remember: In a specific sequence, use one factor for each trial.
concepts.commonMistake: The formula assumes the same p on every trial and independence across trials.

concepts.title: Exactly k successes
concepts.explanation: The event “exactly k successes” contains many distinct patterns. First calculate the probability of one pattern. Then count the choices of the k success positions using C(n,k). The patterns are disjoint and have equal probability, so their probabilities add. The assumptions are a fixed number n of independent trials with the same success probability p.

example.title: Exactly two replies
example.situation: Four customers independently reply with probability 1/2.
walkthrough: Choose which two customers reply: C(4,2)=6 choices.
Each exact reply pattern has probability (1/2)⁴=1/16.
P(exactly two replies)=6/16=3/8.
example.result: The combination factor accounts for every ordering of the successes.

concepts.remember: “Exactly k” means count all sequences with k successes.
concepts.commonMistake: Using only pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ gives one specific ordering, not all possible orderings.

concepts.title: At least one success
concepts.explanation: Zero successes means every trial fails. For n independent trials with common success probability p, that single pattern has probability (1 − p)ⁿ. Subtracting it from 1 includes every possible positive success count. If success probabilities differ but independence holds, replace the power with the product of the individual failure probabilities.

example.title: Reaching a server
example.situation: Each of three independent attempts succeeds with probability 0.2.
walkthrough: P(one attempt fails)=0.8.
P(all three fail)=0.8³=0.512.
P(at least one succeeds)=1−0.512=0.488.
example.result: A complement avoids adding the cases of exactly one, two, and three successes.

concepts.remember: For “at least one,” calculate “none” first.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not multiply p three times; p³ is the probability that all three succeed.

concepts.title: Series and parallel systems
concepts.explanation: A series system works only when all its components work. A parallel system works when at least one component works. For independent component states, multiply success probabilities for series; multiply failure probabilities and subtract from 1 for parallel. A shared power failure or common environmental hazard can invalidate that independence assumption.
concepts.formula: Series: ∏ᵢ pᵢ   ·   Parallel: 1−∏ᵢ(1−pᵢ), for independent components

example.title: Two ways to connect the same equipment
example.situation: Two components work independently with probabilities 0.9 and 0.8. Compare a process that needs both components with a backup arrangement that needs either one.
walkthrough: Series: both must work, so P(success) = 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72.
Parallel: failure requires both to fail, so P(failure) = 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02.
Thus parallel success is 1 − 0.02 = 0.98. The component probabilities are unchanged; the success requirement changed.
example.result: The same components give 72% series reliability or 98% parallel reliability under independence.

concepts.remember: Translate the system rule into “all” or “at least one” before calculating.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not add component reliability directly; the components’ working events can overlap.
concepts.definition: A parallel subsystem succeeds if any one of its components succeeds, so its probability of failure is the product of the probabilities of failure of the corresponding components

quickChecks.prompt: Four fair coin tosses produce exactly two heads with what probability?
quickChecks.explanation: There are C(4,2)=6 matching sequences, each with probability 1/16.

quickChecks.prompt: Two independent components work with probabilities 0.9 and 0.8. If both are required, what is system reliability?
quickChecks.explanation: A series system needs both, so multiply 0.9×0.8.

lessons.title: Counting
lessons.subtitle: Count possibilities before assigning probabilities
lessons.introduction: Count outcomes by constructing them in stages. Decide whether order, replacement, and group labels matter before choosing a formula. Counting supplies probabilities only when the relevant outcomes are equally likely.
objectives: Apply the multiplication principle to sequential choices.
Distinguish permutations, ordered selections, and combinations.
Count group assignments and arrangements with repeated items.

concepts.title: The multiplication principle
concepts.explanation: Break the construction of one outcome into stages. If stage 1 has n₁ choices and every partial choice has n₂ continuations at stage 2, there are n₁n₂ pairs. Extend this to more stages by multiplying. The number of continuations at a given stage must be the same for every earlier history; otherwise count the branches separately. This principle counts possibilities, without requiring probabilistic independence.
concepts.formula: Total choices = choices at stage 1 × choices at stage 2 × ···

example.title: Creating a short access code
example.situation: A code uses one of 3 letters followed by one of 4 digits.
walkthrough: Choose the letter in 3 ways.
For each letter, choose the digit in 4 ways.
There are 3×4=12 codes.
example.result: Multiply when every option at one stage can be followed by every option at the next.

concepts.remember: Draw a few branches if you are unsure whether stages multiply.
concepts.commonMistake: Addition is for alternative cases; multiplication is for successive choices within one construction.
concepts.definition: The counting principle is based on a divide-and-conquer approach, whereby the counting is broken down into stages through the use of a tree.

concepts.title: Subsets
concepts.explanation: To form a subset of n distinct objects, decide separately at each counting stage whether to include that object. There are two choices at each of n stages, giving 2ⁿ subsets. This count includes the empty subset and the full set. It is a count of possible selections, not a claim that a real selection procedure makes all subsets equally likely.
concepts.formula: Number of subsets of an n-element set = 2ⁿ

example.title: Optional pizza toppings
example.situation: Five toppings can each be included or excluded.
walkthrough: Every topping gives 2 choices.
Multiply across five toppings: 2×2×2×2×2.
There are 2⁵=32 possible topping sets, including none and all five.
example.result: A subset problem is often a sequence of yes/no choices.

concepts.remember: The empty subset and the full set count unless the question excludes them.
concepts.commonMistake: Counting only nonempty choices changes 2ⁿ to 2ⁿ−1.

concepts.title: Permutations
concepts.explanation: A permutation places distinct objects in order. With no repetition, n choices are available for the first position, n − 1 for the second, and so on. Filling all n positions gives n!. Filling only k gives n!/(n − k)!. Decide what makes objects and positions distinct before choosing the formula.
concepts.formula: Number of orders of n distinct objects = n!

example.title: Books on a shelf
example.situation: Four different books are arranged in one row.
walkthrough: There are 4 choices for the first position.
Then 3, 2, and 1 choices remain.
The number of arrangements is 4!=4×3×2×1=24.
example.result: Changing the order creates a new arrangement.

concepts.remember: Use n! when all n distinct objects are placed into ordered positions.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not use n! for an unordered group; most of those orders represent the same group.

concepts.title: Ordered selections versus combinations
concepts.explanation: A combination selects a group without assigning positions. Ordered selections count every group k! times, once for each internal ordering. Divide n!/(n − k)! by k! to count each group once. Use combinations when exchanging two selected objects leaves the outcome unchanged; use ordered selections when their roles matter.

example.title: President and secretary versus a two-person team
example.situation: Five people are available.
walkthrough: President and secretary: 5×4=20 assignments because swapping roles changes the result.
A two-person team: C(5,2)=10 because swapping names does not create a new team.
The ordered count is 2!=2 times the unordered count.
example.result: Ask whether the selected positions have different labels.

concepts.remember: If swapping selected objects changes the outcome, order matters.
concepts.commonMistake: Words such as “choose” do not guarantee a combination; named roles make the selection ordered.
concepts.definition: Notice that forming a combination is different than forming a k-permutation, because in a combination there is no ordering of the selected elements.

concepts.title: Allocations to labelled groups
concepts.explanation: To divide n distinct objects into labelled groups of fixed sizes n₁,…,nᵣ, choose the first group, then the second from the remaining objects, and continue. The product simplifies to n!/(n₁!⋯nᵣ!), where the sizes sum to n. The labels matter: “morning team” and “evening team” are different roles. Reordering people within the same group does not create a new allocation.

example.title: Assigning a six-person support team
example.situation: Six distinct staff members must be assigned to labelled shifts: two in the morning, three in the afternoon, and one in the evening. Order within a shift does not matter.
walkthrough: Choose the morning pair: C(6,2) = 15 possibilities.
From the remaining four staff, choose three for the afternoon: C(4,3) = 4. The remaining person takes the evening shift.
Multiply: 15 × 4 × 1 = 60. Equivalently, 6!/(2!3!1!) = 60.
example.result: There are 60 allocations to the three labelled shifts.

concepts.remember: The groups have distinct labels; order within a group does not matter.
concepts.commonMistake: Do not divide again for swapping morning and afternoon teams: their different shift labels make different allocations.

concepts.title: Arrangements with repeated labels
concepts.explanation: When some objects have identical labels, swapping those identical labels does not produce a new visible arrangement. Temporarily treat all objects as distinct, count their orders, then divide by the internal permutations of each repeated label. This gives the same factorial ratio as assigning positions to labelled groups.

example.title: Arranging three parcel labels
example.situation: A packing display uses three labels in a row: A, A, and B. Only the printed letters matter.
walkthrough: If the A labels were marked A₁ and A₂, all three labels would be distinct and there would be 3! = 6 orders.
Erasing the subscripts makes each visible order occur twice, because A₁ and A₂ can trade places.
Divide by 2!: 6/2 = 3. The visible arrangements are AAB, ABA, and BAA.
example.result: There are 3 different visible label sequences.

concepts.remember: Divide only for swaps that leave the observed arrangement unchanged.
concepts.commonMistake: If the two A labels were distinguishable in a way the question records, dividing by 2! would be incorrect.

quickChecks.prompt: From five people, how many ways can you choose an unordered team of two?
quickChecks.explanation: Use C(5,2)=10 because the two positions are not labeled.

quickChecks.prompt: How many distinct arrangements does AAB have?
quickChecks.explanation: Start with 3!=6 and divide by 2! for the repeated A: 6/2=3.
